verses.text: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews.
He came to Jesus at night and said, "Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God. For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him."
Jesus replied, "Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again."
"How can a man be born when he is old?" Nicodemus asked. "Can he enter his mother's womb a second time to be born?"
Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit.
Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit.
Do not be amazed that I said, 'You must be born again.'
The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit."
"How can this be?" Nicodemus asked.
"You are Israel's teacher," said Jesus, "and you do not understand these things?
Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and yet you people do not accept our testimony.
If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?
No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven—the Son of Man.
Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,
that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.
For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.
For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him.
Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God's one and only Son.
And this is the verdict: The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light because their deeds were evil.
Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed.
But whoever practices the truth comes into the Light, so that it may be seen clearly that what he has done has been accomplished in God."
After this, Jesus and His disciples went into the Judean countryside, where He spent some time with them and baptized.
Now John was also baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there, and people kept coming to be baptized.
(For John had not yet been thrown into prison.)
Then a dispute arose between John's disciples and a certain Jew over the issue of ceremonial washing.
So John's disciples came to him and said, "Look, Rabbi, the One who was with you beyond the Jordan, the One you testified about—He is baptizing, and everyone is going to Him."
John replied, "A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.
You yourselves can testify that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but am sent ahead of Him.'
The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom stands and listens for him, and is overjoyed to hear the bridegroom's voice. That joy is mine, and it is now complete.
He must increase; I must decrease.
The One who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth belongs to the earth and speaks as one from the earth. The One who comes from heaven is above all.
He testifies to what He has seen and heard, yet no one accepts His testimony.
Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful.
For the One whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for God gives the Spirit without limit.
The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him."

context.author: Traditionally the apostle John
context.genre: Theological narrative — an extended private discourse followed by John the Baptist's final recorded testimony
context.audience: A broad, likely mixed Jewish and Gentile readership toward the end of the first century
context.setting: The chapter opens somewhere in Jerusalem, likely just after the temple cleansing of chapter 2, then shifts to the Judean countryside where Jesus' disciples baptize, and to Aenon near Salim in the Jordan Valley, where John continued his own ministry.
context.custom: Approaching a rabbi privately at night wasn't unusual for a serious student wanting uninterrupted time, though Nicodemus's caution as a prominent Sanhedrin member also likely reflects real risk to his public standing. The role John describes for himself, "friend of the bridegroom," was a recognized wedding office responsible for arranging the ceremony and rejoicing in the couple's joy rather than claiming any of it for himself.
context.timelineImmediate: This extended conversation with Nicodemus is followed by a short summary of Jesus' own baptizing ministry in Judea, then by what becomes John the Baptist's last recorded words in this Gospel — a deliberate, joyful stepping back as Jesus' ministry grows.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' image of being "lifted up" like the bronze serpent draws directly on Numbers 21:4-9, where Israelites bitten by venomous snakes were healed simply by looking at a bronze serpent Moses raised on a pole — a strange, specific Old Testament sign Jesus applies directly to His own coming crucifixion.
context.sparkNotes: A Pharisee named Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night, and their conversation produces both the concept of being "born again" and the single most quoted verse in the whole Bible, John 3:16. The chapter closes with John the Baptist's last recorded words in this Gospel, gladly stepping back from the spotlight with the line, "He must increase; I must decrease."

translation.meaning: The Greek word anōthen genuinely carries both senses at once — "again" and "from above" — which is likely exactly why Nicodemus misunderstands Jesus as talking about a literal second physical birth.
The ordered created world, humanity as a whole — a strikingly universal scope for a Jewish audience that often expected God's rescue to be for Israel specifically.

occurrences.note: John uses this word far more than any other New Testament writer — it's one of his signature terms.

translation.meaning: Not simply endless duration, but a whole different quality of life belonging to God's own kingdom — a life John presents as already available now to whoever believes, not only after death.
translation.gloss: Life of the age to come

otBackground.note: The bronze serpent lifted up by Moses in the wilderness — directly applied by Jesus to His own coming crucifixion.
God's promise of cleansing water and a new heart given by His Spirit — background for Jesus' language of being born "of water and the Spirit."
Abraham's willingness to give up his only son Isaac — echoed in God's own giving of His "one and only Son" in v.16.

commentary.note: Henry reads Nicodemus's nighttime visit sympathetically but honestly: 'Nicodemus was afraid, or ashamed to be seen with Christ, therefore came in the night... though he came by night, yet afterward he owned Christ publicly.' On God's love in v.16, he writes simply, 'behold, and wonder, that the great God should love such a worthless world.'

Poole reads John the Baptist's 'he must increase' through the image John himself had already used of the morning star giving way to sunrise: 'he is the rising sun... he must shine every day more and more. But I must decrease... I must every day decay, and grow less and less, as Christ increaseth.' A willing, joyful fading rather than a bitter one.

Gill notes the real historical shape of John's decrease: not just in public esteem, but quite literally in circumstance — 'quickly after this he was put into prison, and there put to death.' His willing decrease wasn't abstract humility; it led directly and soon to his own execution.

Lewis does not comment on John 3 verse by verse, but "Making and Begetting" in Mere Christianity explains why Jesus is called the only begotten Son (v.16). He says that to beget is to bring forth something of the same kind as yourself, while to make is to produce something different, like a man who begets a child but builds a statue. He then argues that the new birth in verses 3-8 is meant to turn creatures into sons, a different kind of life from the one we have by nature. (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)

overview.summary: At night Nicodemus, a Pharisee, visits Jesus, who tells him he must be born from above. Jesus explains that God so loved the world that He gave His Son, and John the Baptist says he must decrease while Jesus increases.
overview.settingLine: Jerusalem at night, then the Judean countryside.

history.t: A member of the Sanhedrin and a respected teacher of Israel.
Jesus' disciples and John both baptized at once, which stirred rivalry.

customs.t: Teachers often studied by night, away from crowds and scrutiny.
Hebrew and Greek use one word for wind, breath and spirit.

archaeology.t: Stepped ritual baths are found across Jerusalem from this period.
A water tunnel still runs beneath the old city from the Gihon Spring.

overview.discussion: Jesus told Nicodemus he must be born again. What does a fresh start look like for someone already religious?
overview.book: The fourth Gospel · 21 chapters. Written so readers would believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.
overview.author: John
